title: A member the provider is throttling is marked stuck: the ladder answers a rate limit with continues and a restart that re-send the same context
foundBy: session agent operating two eight-member campaigns side by side on one host, reading every member's own CLI session records after both campaigns had ended
details:
**What happened.** Three members of two campaigns were marked `node-stuck` with `2 continues and 1 restarts spent`. None had crashed. Each machine was up with memory free, its CLI processes were alive, and the kernel log held no kill. Every failed turn of all three ends on the provider's error, in the CLI's own session record. The error is a rate limit on tokens per minute, and it asks the caller to try again in 6 to 18 seconds.

**The mechanism, in four steps.**

1. Several members share one provider key. An agent loop makes a request every ten seconds or so, and each request re-sends the member's whole context. With contexts of 130,000 to 245,000 tokens, one member can ask for more in a minute than the key's per-minute allowance. Several together sit at the allowance for the whole campaign. Cached input was counted toward the limit in full.
2. The CLI retries about five times over roughly a minute, then ends the turn with the error and no reply. The turn driver reports that turn as finished (filed in the sandbox ledger as SBX-044).
3. `protocol.Compute` sees an open dispatch, no reply and no live driver, and returns `node-stopped` with `NextMove: "continue"`. The orchestrator's `wait` delivers the continue, in one case six seconds after the turn ended.
4. The continue's first effect is that the member sends its whole context again, into the same exhausted minute. It fails the same way. Two continues and a restart went in 21 minutes for one member and 25 for another. The restart is the worst rung for this failure, because it wipes the session. The member then re-reads its brief and its whole dispatch thread, and it rebuilds the same large context before it does any work.

**Why the protocol's own reasoning does not cover this.** PROTOCOL.md says *"The ladder replaces diagnosis"*, because a node that stopped and a session that wedged *"are not distinguishable by observation"*, and for those two causes retrying is the cure. A throttle is a third cause, it **is** distinguishable, because the CLI's session record names it, and retrying is not the cure: retrying is the load. The ladder's two remedies both make it worse.

**What it cost.** In one campaign a member was lost before it had committed anything. The orchestrator's only available recovery was to give that member's job to a member with different mounts. That defeated a hold-out the team's design depended on. About two hours of a campaign of under four were spent waiting on turns the provider then ended. The orchestrators behaved correctly throughout: a member inside its ladder is, as far as they can know, working.

**How to reproduce, without a real limit.** Give a member a provider base URL that answers every model call with the provider's rate-limit response for longer than the CLI's retry budget. A local stub is enough. Dispatch to it. Expected today: the turn ends without a reply, `observe` shows `node-stopped · continue next`, the continues and the restart are delivered minutes apart, and the member ends `node-stuck` while its machine is healthy. This reproduction is described from the observed behaviour and from reading `internal/protocol/state.go`; it has not been run against a stub.

**What would fix it.** A turn that ended on a provider throttle should cost a wait and not a rung. The harness should back off, with jitter, for at least as long as the provider asked. It should neither count a continue nor ever reach the restart. The elapsed bound can still apply, so a member cannot wait forever. That needs the turn's end to carry a reason, which is SAC-035. Until then the campaign's own policy is the only lever, and a longer ladder only moves the cliff: the defaults were spent in minutes against a condition that lasted hours.

notes.text: The reproduction the record could only describe now runs with no machine. A scripted provider throttles one agent for forty minutes while the real wait loop runs on a simulated clock. The agent is charged two continues and one restart, and it is stuck fifteen minutes after its dispatch opened. This record is now worked as one stint with every record marked `reliability-2026-09`, which includes the three filed today. They share one cause, which is that the harness knows too little about why a node is quiet. The sandbox's turn drivers now report a failure class and whether an agent is in a turn. The plan is to read both from the node's own machine.
